title: 2. Numeracy & Number Systems: One-to-One Correspondence in Counting
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the number of objects in a collection when each object is matched with exactly one partner.
questions.question: In a row of \(5\) chairs, each chair has exactly one child sitting on it. How many children are sitting on the chairs?
questions.explanation: Each chair is matched with exactly one child, and every chair is occupied. Therefore, the number of children is the same as the number of chairs: \(5\). So there are \(5\) children.
questions.hint: Match each chair with one child and compare the two groups.

questions.learningObjective: Identify when two finite collections can be matched one-to-one.
questions.question: A basket has \(3\) apples. A plate has \(3\) oranges. Which statement is true about matching the apples and oranges one-to-one?

options.label: A
options.text: There are more apples than oranges.

options.label: B
options.text: Each apple can be matched with exactly one orange.

questions.explanation: The basket has \(3\) apples and the plate has \(3\) oranges. Since the two collections have the same number of objects, each apple can be paired with exactly one orange, with none left over. Therefore, the true statement is that each apple can be matched with exactly one orange.
questions.hint: Compare the two counts and see whether each object in one group can be paired with one object in the other group.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the number of unmatched objects after forming one-to-one pairs.
questions.question: A row has \(6\) cups and a row has \(6\) saucers. If each cup is matched with one saucer, how many saucers are left unmatched?
questions.explanation: There are \(6\) cups and \(6\) saucers. Matching each cup with one saucer uses all \(6\) cups and all \(6\) saucers. Since the two groups have the same number, no saucer is left unmatched. Therefore, the number of unmatched saucers is \(0\).
questions.hint: Pair each cup with one saucer, then check whether any saucer remains without a partner.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the result of attempting a one-to-one match between two unequal collections.
questions.question: There are \(7\) pencils and \(5\) erasers. If we try to match each pencil with one eraser, what happens?
questions.explanation: There are more pencils than erasers: \(7\) pencils and \(5\) erasers. Matching each eraser with one pencil uses all \(5\) erasers, but \(7-5=2\) pencils remain without an eraser. Therefore, \(2\) pencils cannot be matched.
questions.hint: Compare the two counts and identify which group has more objects.

questions.concept: One-to-One Correspondence and Cardinality in Counting
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the final number word in a correct count as the total number of objects.
questions.question: A child points to each block exactly once while counting in order: \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), \(5\), \(6\), \(7\), \(8\). What does the final number \(8\) tell us about the collection?
questions.explanation: In correct counting, each block is matched with exactly one number word, and the number words are said in order. The child points to each block exactly once and finishes with \(8\). The final number word tells how many objects are in the whole collection. Therefore, the collection contains exactly \(8\) blocks.
questions.hint: Each block was matched with exactly one number word. What does the last number word said tell you?

questions.learningObjective: Determine which collection has an unmatched object after one collection is increased.
questions.question: Mia matches \(4\) red counters with \(4\) blue counters. Then she adds \(1\) red counter. If she keeps the same matching, which group has an unmatched counter?

options.label: A
options.text: The red group has \(1\) unmatched counter.

options.label: B
options.text: The blue group has \(1\) unmatched counter.

questions.explanation: At first, there are \(4\) red counters and \(4\) blue counters, so they can be matched one-to-one. After Mia adds \(1\) red counter, there are \(5\) red counters and \(4\) blue counters. The \(4\) blue counters can match with \(4\) of the red counters, leaving \(5-4=1\) red counter unmatched. Therefore, the red group has \(1\) unmatched counter.
questions.hint: After adding one red counter, compare the new number of red counters with the number of blue counters.

questions.learningObjective: Infer equality of two collections when each member of one collection receives exactly one item and none remain.
questions.question: A teacher gives each of \(9\) students one sticker. The teacher uses \(9\) stickers and has none left. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: There are more stickers than students.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of stickers equals the number of students.

questions.explanation: Each of the \(9\) students receives exactly one sticker, and no sticker is left over. This forms a one-to-one match between the \(9\) students and the stickers used. Therefore, the number of stickers must equal the number of students, which is \(9\).
questions.hint: Imagine pairing each student with the sticker they received. Is any student or any sticker left without a partner?

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether two collections of different shapes can be matched one-to-one based on their counts.
questions.question: A row has \(6\) triangles. A second row has \(6\) squares. A student says, "I can match each triangle with exactly one square." Is the student correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because both rows have the same number of objects.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because triangles and squares are different shapes.

questions.explanation: One-to-one correspondence depends on whether each object in one collection can be paired with exactly one object in the other collection. Both rows have \(6\) objects. Therefore, each of the \(6\) triangles can be matched with exactly one of the \(6\) squares, even though the shapes are different. The student is correct.
questions.hint: Count the objects in each row. What must be true about the two counts for every triangle to get exactly one square?

questions.learningObjective: Determine the number of containers needed when each object is placed into exactly one container.
questions.question: There are \(10\) beads in a bag. Each bead is placed into exactly one small box. After all beads are placed, every box contains exactly one bead and no bead remains. How many boxes were used?
questions.explanation: Each bead is placed into exactly one box, and every box contains exactly one bead. This creates a one-to-one match between the \(10\) beads and the boxes used. Since no bead remains, the number of boxes must equal the number of beads, which is \(10\).
questions.hint: Imagine pairing each bead with its box. Could there be a box without a bead, or a bead without a box?

questions.learningObjective: Identify an error in counting caused by matching one object with more than one number word.
questions.question: A collection has \(7\) counters. A student points to each counter and says, "\(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), \(5\), \(6\), \(7\)." Then the student points again to a counter that was already counted and says, "\(8\)." Which statement best describes the counting?

options.label: A
options.text: The count \(8\) is correct because the student said one more number.

options.label: B
options.text: The count \(8\) is incorrect because one counter was matched with two number words.

questions.explanation: Correct counting requires one-to-one correspondence: each counter must be matched with exactly one number word. The student first counts the \(7\) counters correctly, but then points again to a counter that was already counted and says "\(8\)." This gives one counter two number words, so the one-to-one correspondence is broken. Therefore, the count \(8\) is incorrect.
questions.hint: Check whether every counter is paired with exactly one number word and no counter is counted twice.
